title: 230V / 220V Watts to Amps Calculator | Wattlyst
meta: Convert watts to amps on 230V or 220V mains. Power factor included, with a table for common appliances like ACs, irons and water motors.
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: 220 V amps calculator: is 220 V different from 230 V?
p: Barely. Pakistan's standard supply is 230 V, but many appliance labels and older guides say 220 V. The same 1,000 W load draws 4.55 A at 220 V and a little less at 230 V, a difference smaller than the day-to-day swing of the mains itself. Pick whichever voltage your label shows; a 220V and a 230V calculation lead to the same wire and breaker choice.
The 120 V option is for the US and Canada, where the same watts draw roughly twice the amps. That is why a 120 V heater needs a much thicker cable than a 230 V one.

sections.h2: How many amps is 1,500 watts at 230 V?
p: It depends on the power factor. A 1,500 W heating load (power factor one) draws 6.52 A at 230 V. A 1,500 W load with a power factor of 0.8, typical of an AC, fridge or a mixed set of appliances, draws 8.15 A. Same watts, about a quarter more current.

This is why an appliance's current is sometimes printed as a higher figure than watts ÷ volts. The label amps include the reactive part of the load, which the meter does not bill but the wire must carry.

sections.h2: AC amps at 230 V: why the power factor changes the answer
p: A 1.5 ton inverter AC runs at about 1,450 W. With a power factor of 0.8 that is 7.88 A at 230 V. A non-inverter AC of the same size runs at more watts and also starts with a surge of several times its running current for a second or two, which is what trips an undersized breaker. Use the running amps for the cable and the generator and breaker tools for the surge.

Resistive loads are simpler. An electric iron of about 1,000 W, a 2,000 W kettle or a geyser all have a power factor of one, so their current is just watts ÷ volts. That is why the table below lists the power factor next to each row.

sections.h2: Three-phase and 120 V: the same calculator for other supplies
p: Switch the supply type to three-phase and choose the 400 V line-to-line option. The formula gains a factor of the square root of three because the load is spread over three wires: 5,000 W at a power factor of 0.8 draws 9.02 A per line. Enter the line-to-line voltage (400 V in Pakistan), not the phase-to-neutral 230 V.

Most homes in Pakistan are single-phase; a three-phase connection is normal for large houses, shops and motors. If you are checking whether a load fits a single-phase meter, the single phase load calculator does that job.

faq.q: How many amps is 1,000 watts at 220 V?
faq.a: 1,000 W ÷ (220 V × a power factor of one) = 4.55 A for a heating load such as an iron. For a motor or AC with a power factor of about 0.8, the current is about a quarter higher.

faq.q: How many amps does a 2,000 W heater draw at 230 V?
faq.a: 8.7 A. A heater is a pure resistive load with a power factor of one, so the current is simply 2,000 W ÷ 230 V, and it draws that for as long as the element is on.

faq.q: How many amps does an iron draw at 230 V?
faq.a: A typical dry or steam iron is about 1,000 W, which is 4.55 A at 220 V and a touch less at 230 V. Bigger steam irons are rated higher, so check the label.

faq.q: What is the 230 V current calculation formula?
faq.a: Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). For a 1,500 W load at 230 V and a power factor of 0.8, that is 8.15 A. For three-phase, multiply the line-to-line voltage by the square root of three as well.

faq.q: How many amps does a 1.5 ton AC draw at 230 V?
faq.a: A 1.5 ton inverter AC running at about 1,450 W with a power factor of 0.8 draws 7.88 A. A non-inverter unit runs at more watts and briefly surges to several times that when the compressor starts.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator for 120 V?
faq.a: Yes. Choose the 120 V option for US and Canadian supplies. The same watts draw roughly twice the amps of a 230 V supply, which is why appliances there need thicker cable and higher-rated breakers.

faq.q: How many amps is 5,000 W on three-phase 400 V?
faq.a: 9.02 A per line at a power factor of 0.8. Three-phase divides the load across three wires, so each carries far less than the same load would on a single phase.

faq.q: Which wire and breaker do I need for these amps?
faq.a: Use the running amps with the wire size calculator, which adds the cable length and voltage drop, and the breaker size calculator for the MCB. Both keep a margin above the running current; a licensed electrician should confirm the final choice.

key_facts: On a 230 V single-phase supply, amps = watts ÷ (230 × power factor); at a power factor of 0.8, 1,500 W draws 8.15 A.
A 2,000 W heater, iron or kettle (power factor one) draws 8.7 A at 230 V; a 1,450 W 1.5 ton inverter AC at a power factor of 0.8 draws 7.88 A.
1,000 W at 220 V and a power factor of one is 4.55 A; at 230 V the same load draws slightly less, so a 220V label and a 230V supply give almost the same answer.
Three-phase at 400 V line to line spreads the load over three wires: 5,000 W at a power factor of 0.8 is 9.02 A per line.
mistakes: Using a power factor of one for an AC, fridge or water motor. Their current is about a quarter higher than watts ÷ volts; use about 0.8 unless the label says otherwise.
Using the phase-to-neutral 230 V with the three-phase formula. Three-phase needs the line-to-line voltage (400 V in Pakistan) and the square root of three.

Taking the running amps of a non-inverter AC or motor as its only current. The compressor or pump surges to several times this for a moment at start-up, which is what trips breakers and stalls generators.
Buying a breaker or wire equal to the calculated amps. Cables and MCBs need a margin above the running current; use the wire size and breaker size calculators for the final choice.

examples.title: 1,000 watts at 220 V (an electric iron)
examples.text: 1,000 W ÷ (220 V × 1) = 4.55 A. An iron is a pure heating load, so the power factor is one.

examples.title: A 2,000 W heater or kettle at 230 V
examples.text: 2,000 W ÷ (230 V × 1) = 8.7 A. A room heater, kettle or hot plate of 2,000 W draws 8.7 A continuously while it runs.

examples.title: 1,500 watts at 230 V, power factor one
examples.text: 1,500 W ÷ (230 V × 1) = 6.52 A for a heating load. The same 1,500 W with a power factor of 0.8 draws more; try it in the calculator.

examples.title: A 1.5 ton inverter AC at 230 V
examples.text: A 1.5 ton inverter AC runs at about 1,450 W. 1,450 W ÷ (230 V × 0.8) = 7.88 A running current. Starting is gentle for an inverter AC; a non-inverter AC surges well above this.

examples.title: 5,000 W on a three-phase 400 V supply
examples.text: 5,000 W ÷ (√3 × 400 V × 0.8) = 9.02 A per line. The square root of three appears because three-phase power is shared across three wires.

formula.text: I = P ÷ (V × PF)  (single-phase);  I = P ÷ (√3 × V × PF)  (three-phase)
lines: V = supply voltage: 230 V single-phase, 400 V line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor, 1 for heating loads, about 0.8 for motors, ACs and mixed loads

content.safety: The amps from this page decide cable and breaker size, so never pick a wire or MCB from this result alone. Add the margins the wiring calculators use and have a licensed electrician check and connect any new circuit.
